planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown own-root plants against a wall, fence, or into a tree in spring or fall; this vigorous rambler needs a large, sturdy structure to climb rather than a small trellis.

directions: Bred by Antoine A. Jacques in France around 1827, this Hybrid Sempervirens rambler produces dense clusters of small, fully double, creamy-white rosette flowers that open from distinctly pink-tinged buds, with a light primrose-like fragrance. Its slender, nearly thornless red-green canes carry glossy, semi-evergreen foliage and bloom in a single heavy flush in early summer, followed by small orange-red hips in fall. The scrambling growth habit and tolerance of partial shade make it well suited to covering walls, arbors, or old trees where sturdier climbers would struggle, though it needs a once-a-year framework tidy after bloom rather than hard annual pruning. It is also the parent of the dwarf, repeat-blooming 1879 sport 'Little White Pet'.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and sharply drained soil; this near-black self is one of three cultivars to share the American Iris Society's 2025 Wister Medal.

directions: Bred by Keith Keppel and registered in 2018, Dark Universe is an early-blooming tall bearded iris carrying deep, velvety concord-purple standards and falls so dark they read as near-black in the garden, with only the faintest blue-white edge and a small lightly speckled area beside the beard breaking the solid color. It earned the American Iris Society's Honorable Mention in 2021, Award of Merit in 2023, and shared the 2025 Wister Medal, recognition of its striking color and dependable rebloom in gardens across the country. Plant rhizomes high and shallow in a lean, well-drained bed, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly with tops exposed in late summer to early fall in full sun and sharply drained soil; this chocolate-and-white plicata is named for the San Francisco chocolate-factory shopping complex and shares the AIS's 2025 Wister Medal with Keppel's own 'Dark Universe'.

directions: Bred by Keith Keppel and registered in 2015, Ghirardelli Square is an early-midseason tall bearded iris with a reddish-chocolate and white plicata pattern: blended brown standards, brown style arms washed with wax yellow, and white falls edged in a wide band of purple-chocolate stippling that bleeds inward with fine dark veining beside a mustard-tan beard. It earned the American Iris Society's Honorable Mention in 2018 and Award of Merit in 2021 before sharing the 2025 Wister Medal alongside two other cultivars, since the AIS has awarded three Wister Medal winners per year since 1998 given how competitive the tall bearded class is. Plant rhizomes high and shallow in lean, well-drained soil and divide every three to four years after bloom.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall so roots establish before winter in rich, well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun.

directions: Hybridized by O. David Niswonger from a cross involving 'Far Out' and 'Redwood Supreme' and registered in 1996, Missouri Autumn bears a self-colored light brown flower on tall, sturdy stems above sword-like foliage at midseason, an understated but luminous shade that catalog descriptions note seems to light up when viewed from across the garden. It went on to win the American Iris Society's Honorable Mention in 2001, Award of Merit in 2005, and the Nies Medal (the top award for spuria irises) in 2009. Keep soil consistently moist from fall through the spring bloom period, then let it dry out during midsummer dormancy, since spurias are prone to rhizome rot if kept wet while resting. Established clumps resent disturbance and should be divided only every four to six years.
